item.title: The Utter Predictability of the Nvidia/Jensen Huang Debacle
item.description:
Infidelity

The Utter Predictability of the Nvidia/Jensen Huang Debacle

Surely psychologists aren’t the only ones unsurprised by the Nvidia scandal.

Posted November 12, 2026

Key points
  • Personality traits like humility and honesty predict cheating in relationships.
  • Situational forces like having money or power also make infidelity more likely for some than others.
  • Affairs seem to be more of an occupational hazard for certain types of jobs.

It’s not every day that an email makes international news before toppling global stock markets and beheading the organizational chart of one of tech's household names. But if you’re Jensen Huang admitting to at least one extramarital affair to all 40,000+ employees of Nvidia, this all makes too much sense.

After 33 years at Nvidia, everything changed for Jensen Huang in just three days.
Source: Mariia Berezovsky / Unsplash

Since the story broke about the married-with-children billionaire CEO behind the world’s most powerful AI company sleeping with not only an alleged Chinese spy, but also an employee, the internet has gone giddy with memes, commentary, and endless speculation about what goes on inside closed rooms–bedrooms and boardrooms alike. I’ll leave the economists to make predictions about the future of the AI market without its most famous CEO at the helm and politicians to quibble about what this means for U.S.-China ties going forward. As a psychologist, though, I think now is a good time to revisit the long-established predictors of marital fidelity, which is less of a black box and more of a formula.

Personality Matters (as Much as the Situation)

Much investigative journalism has gone into the dark and mysterious convergence of events leading to Huang meeting and subsequently falling for Alice Huang, the presumed Chinese operative, as well as the more quotidian circumstances that led to his affair with Kimberly Powell, his executive and subordinate. But as much as extenuating situations can promote infidelity, personality matters too.

A while back, researchers conducted a series of studies to show just how well a person’s humility and honesty predicted their capacity to lie in their romantic relationships. Tech billionaires are known for many things, but humility is not one of them. Curiously, the research on humility and relationship dishonesty also found that proud/dishonest people should also be more likely to suspect their relationship partners’ dishonesty (thanks to our tendency to project ourselves onto others). But in the Jensen case, he did appear to defy this trend when he failed to be suspicious of his spy-mistress.

Power and Money Have a Hard Time (Being Innocent)

Of course, the personality traits that made Jensen into both a billionaire and a bad husband are only part of the equation. The situation always matters, and the link between power and cheating has long been established. Time and again, studies have shown that people who naturally have more power or are temporarily made to feel more powerful are more likely to cheat on their relationship partners.

As Lex Luthor once said, the oldest lie in America is that power can be innocent.
Source: Cottonbro studio / Pexels

While this trend is in part because power makes you more impulsive, likely to act, self-focused, and psychologically distant from other people, it’s also moderated by beliefs. Because people like to validate themselves, power seems to have these negative effects on relationship fidelity only when the person has positive thoughts about cheating. For those who think of cheating negatively, power doesn’t make them more likely to be unfaithful.

Money has a similar effect. In one study, men who were made to feel richer were less satisfied with their partner’s physical attractiveness and more likely to approach an attractive woman. Other research has found that being extremely financially focused in general predicts worse relationship satisfaction.

The Group/Organization Can Also Be to Blame

There is at least one more layer to the latest Nvidia scandal: the organizational context. A researcher once called affairs an “occupational hazard” because they were more likely in some organizations than others. Relative to people in other jobs, those in higher administrative positions and in technology were the least likely to say sex with someone other than your spouse was always wrong. This is also consistent with findings from the dating site for married people interested in affairs, AshleyMadison.com, showing that the top industry for their users was IT and Engineering.

Finally, something has to be said about the fact that the Jensen affairs have been years in the making, and the fact that the world is only finding out about it now suggests collusion has been happening this whole time. Psychologists call this collective cheating. While the original work on collective cheating focused on other forms of dishonesty rather than the relational kind, the idea was the same: Sometimes our concern for the group makes us turn a blind eye, and that is at least part of the problem.

item.title: The Art of a Good Life
item.description:
Awe

The Art of a Good Life

Why appreciating beauty may be more important than we think.

Posted November 12, 2026

Key points
  • Appreciating beauty is an important ingredient of a satisfying life.
  • The Harvard Grant Study found appreciation of beauty to be a predictor of life satisfaction.
  • Beauty can inspire awe, connectedness, and prosocial behavior, extending beyond personal pleasure.
Source: Tommao Wang / Unsplash

Most of us are instinctively drawn to beauty. We pause to admire a beautiful landscape, are moved by a piece of music, or find ourselves lingering in front of a painting. Yet, when it comes to life's priorities, beauty and art are often treated as second order: pleasant additions, perhaps, but hardly essential. Worse, an interest in aesthetics can sometimes be dismissed as superficial or unsubstantial, as though paying attention to beauty means neglecting more important things.

I must confess that this attitude has always been rather alien to me. I grew up in a family in which art and culture were considered fundamental ingredients of a good life. My father founded and managed a municipal Endowment of the Arts, and my parents believed deeply in Bildung—the cultivation of the mind and spirit through education and culture. Art deserved time, attention, and space, irrespective of other priorities. It was a human need, not an indulgence. My parents also believed in discernment: Quality mattered, and great art could inspire genuine awe. We went to museums like other people went to church.

But was this simply a cultural inheritance, or is there something more fundamental to the appreciation of beauty? What does science tell us?

Quite a lot, as it turns out.

Life Satisfaction

One particularly intriguing finding comes from the Harvard Grant Study, one of the longest-running studies of adult development. A 2003 paper examined the relationship between personal strengths and life satisfaction across different adult populations, including the surviving men of the Grant Study.

Among these men, two characteristics emerged as significant, independent predictors of life satisfaction: the capacity for loving relationships and the appreciation of beauty.

Think about that for a moment. Appreciation of beauty appeared alongside loving relationships—hardly a trivial companion—as a characteristic associated with a more satisfying life. Beauty, it seems, deserves a place among the ingredients of human flourishing.

The Neuroscience

Source: Tyler Lastovich / Unsplash

Neuroscience offers further clues as to why. Aesthetic experiences are not merely passive visual or sensory events. They engage brain systems involved in pleasure, evaluation, and meaning. A meta-analysis from 2020 examining 49 neuroimaging studies found that appreciating beautiful faces and visual art activated distinct brain regions. The findings suggest that aesthetic appreciation draws on some of the same valuation processes involved in other rewarding experiences, although different forms of beauty engage the brain differently.

Beauty can also inspire awe—that feeling of being confronted with something greater than ourselves. Awe has interesting social consequences. A series of five studies involving more than 2,000 participants found in 2015 that experiences of awe were associated with greater generosity, ethical decision-making, and prosocial behavior. Awe can make our individual concerns feel smaller and connect us to something beyond ourselves. Although these experiments were not specifically about art, they help explain one way in which encounters with beauty may extend beyond personal pleasure.

Engaging With Art

And what about the broader experience of engaging with art? Research has begun to examine how encounters with artistic imagination influence well-being. A 2025 systematic review found that engagement with art and the elevating emotions it generates were associated with emotional well-being, life satisfaction, and meaning in life. Importantly, art engagement need not mean visiting a museum: It can include reading fiction, watching a film, or experiencing theatre.

Source: Szilvia Basso / Unsplash

Taken together, these findings suggest a compelling possibility. Beauty can stimulate our minds and engage our reward systems; it can evoke awe, shift our perspective, and strengthen our sense of connection. Engagement with art, in turn, is associated with greater meaning, life satisfaction, and psychological well-being.

Beauty alone does not deliver a happier life, nor does everyone experience or appreciate beauty in the same way. But this research does challenge the idea that aesthetics is merely decorative.

Perhaps we have been getting our priorities wrong. We devote considerable attention to the things we believe make life good: relationships, achievement, health, and purpose. Yet we may underestimate the contribution of something that can enrich all of them: the capacity to notice, appreciate, and be moved by beauty.

A beautiful painting will not solve our problems. A piece of music will not necessarily make our lives easier. But they can make life feel larger, richer, and more meaningful.

item.title: Five Reasons Marsha Linehan Will Always Be a Legend
item.description:
Borderline Personality Disorder

Five Reasons Marsha Linehan Will Always Be a Legend

How one psychologist transformed the way we understand and treat borderline.

Posted November 12, 2026

Key points
  • Marsha Linehan challenged the belief that BPD was untreatable by developing and testing DBT.
  • She helped clinicians understand the function of challenging behaviors rather than blaming patients.
  • Her legacy lives on through the people she helped and the generations of clinicians she inspired.

The field of clinical psychology lost a giant this week with the passing of Marsha Linehan, the psychologist who developed dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) and fundamentally changed how we understand and treat borderline personality disorder (BPD).

For decades, people with BPD were considered among the most difficult patients to treat. In fact, many clinicians believed that these patients were untreatable. Linehan proved them wrong by developing a better treatment. Since its publication in 1993, DBT has saved countless lives and inspired generations of clinicians and researchers.

As a clinical psychologist whose own career has been shaped by her work, I've been reflecting on what made Linehan such an extraordinary figure. Here are five reasons her legacy will endure.

1. She Went Where Angels Feared to Tread

When Marsha began her work, people experiencing chronic suicidality and severe emotional dysregulation were often viewed as too difficult or too risky to treat. Rather than accepting that these patients couldn't be helped, she set out to develop a treatment that could get the job done.

The result was dialectical behavior therapy, a structured treatment that combined cognitive-behavioral strategies with acceptance-based approaches drawn from Zen practice. DBT taught people practical skills to manage overwhelming emotions, navigate relationships, and build lives worth living.

Marsha was also a scientist who understood the importance of testing whether her approach actually worked. Through rigorous clinical trials, she demonstrated that even people experiencing severe and persistent suicidal behaviors could benefit from treatment.

In doing so, she challenged the longstanding assumption that BPD was untreatable and helped establish a new standard of care.

2. She Changed the Conversation About BPD

Patients with BPD were frequently described as manipulative, attention-seeking, or resistant to treatment.

Marsha challenged these labels by encouraging clinicians to understand the function of behavior. Actions that seemed manipulative or irrational often served a purpose, such as escaping overwhelming emotions or getting important needs met.

Rather than blaming patients for these behaviors, therapists could work to understand what was reinforcing them and teach more effective ways to achieve the same goals.

3. She Got Out of Hell and Went Back to Get Others

In 2011, Marsha publicly shared her own history of severe suffering, suicidality, and psychiatric hospitalization in a New York Times profile.

This revelation had a huge impact. Here was one of the world's most influential clinical psychologists disclosing that she had once experienced profound psychological distress herself.

Marsha later shared more of her story in her memoir, Building a Life Worth Living. She recalled a patient asking her, “Are you one of us?” For people experiencing profound psychological suffering, knowing that someone who had faced similar struggles could go on to build such an extraordinary life offered a powerful source of hope.

She was living proof that recovery was possible.

4. She Taught Us the Power of And

One of Marsha's most important contributions was her emphasis on dialectical thinking, the ability to recognize that two seemingly contradictory things can both be true.

You can accept yourself as you are and work to change.

You can validate someone's suffering and hold them accountable for their behavior.

You can do your best and need to do better.

This was a major shift in how therapists approached treatment. Rather than choosing between validating someone's experience and encouraging them to change, Marsha showed us how to do both. This allowed therapists to approach even the most challenging behaviors with compassion while still helping clients take responsibility for building better lives.

5. She Inspired Generations of Clinicians and Researchers

Marsha's influence extends well beyond the people who received DBT. She trained and inspired generations of clinicians and researchers who have continued building on her work.

I'm one of them.

DBT was the first treatment I learned as a graduate student. Today, I supervise DBT in that same clinic, and Marsha's work continues to shape my own work, BPD Compass.

I first met Marsha when she stopped by my poster at a conference. I was a graduate student presenting BPD research, and I completely fan-girled. It was really cool that she took time to look through the BPD-themed posters and offer encouragement.

Years later, I interviewed with Marsha for a postdoctoral position. Although my career ultimately took me in a different direction, she still agreed to co-mentor my first National Institute of Mental Health grant.

Marsha generously gave her time and encouragement—multiply the experience by the generations of clinicians and researchers she mentored, and you begin to appreciate the reach of her influence.

A Legacy That Will Continue

Marsha Linehan fundamentally changed what clinicians believed was possible for people with BPD by giving them tools that actually worked for these clients.

Despite these advances, too many people with BPD still struggle to access effective treatment. Making effective BPD treatment available to more people is one way we can honor her legacy.

Marsha's influence will live on through the people whose lives she saved and the generations of clinicians and researchers she inspired.

What an extraordinary legacy.

item.title: We Can’t Even Agree on What’s Real, but We Can Still Do This
item.description:
Relationships

We Can’t Even Agree on What’s Real, but We Can Still Do This

A powerful way to cut through confusion and talk across divides.

Posted November 12, 2026

Key points
  • Meaning is slippery. Some argue that words only point to other words—a “free play” without solid grounding.
  • Rather than focusing on meaning, a focus on function can keep conversations moving forward.
  • Asking, "How would that work?" can reduce extremism and over-confidence.
  • Dialogue where judgments are set to one side can create space for richer understanding.
Source: Alex Green/Pexels

Many heated conversations—about everyday topics like medical information and about big topics like foreign policy—seem to wind up challenging our basic understandings of what’s true.

It can feel deeply disturbing to be in a conversation where what seem like basic facts about reality are in question.

In his book Nonduality, philosopher David Loy explains what happened when European thinkers like Jacques Derrida ran into this problem. They discovered that the truth of words and their meanings seems to always rest on the truth of further words and their meanings. It just goes on and on endlessly.

Derrida decided that apparent meaning wasn’t really there. Meaning just depends on other meanings. An idea, when deconstructed, would just lead to other ideas. None of it meant anything definite or universal. Loy calls the result a “free play of discourse.”

That sounds a lot like being on social media today! It can be a frustrating game of continual misunderstandings and endless conflicts about what things mean and what’s true, without much hope of arriving at solid agreement. Have you experienced an interaction like that?

Is everything really meaningless?

We may feel ready to throw up our hands and agree that everything is really meaningless. But that comes with some huge costs.

Luckily, it’s not our only option. There are more interesting ways to address the problem of different ideas about meaning and truth.

One elegant solution comes from the Tibetan scholar and philosopher Tsongkhapa Losang Drakpa. He arrived at a similar conclusion to Derrida that meaning doesn’t rest on anything solid or inherent. But he never gave up on the possibility of shared understanding and experiences. He didn’t accept that everything is equally true (or equally false). Instead, he saw a highly sophisticated solution that can be oversimplified to say that things don’t need to rest on any stable meaning in order to work.

What we need is conventional agreements based on functions. What makes a cup of coffee different from a drawing of a cup of coffee? You can’t drink a drawing. The two have different functions. Focusing on functions can turn an endlessly abstract conversation and debate about meaning into a practical chat.

How would that work?

There’s an easy way to apply this idea in your life the next time someone says something you don’t understand. Move from discussions about what words mean to asking about functions. Ask, “How would that work?” Asking people to describe how their ideas function can get them to reduce overconfidence and tone down extreme beliefs.

Dialogue

Physicist David Bohm, in his book On Dialogue, offered a very different approach. Rather than moving into the practical implications of ideas, he advocated people sitting together until they arrived at “coherence”—a real understanding of one another.

Bohm felt that what was needed was a process to seek real understanding together. This would take a tricky shift. It meant not trying to win and not being stuck on your own thoughts and beliefs. Instead, you had to be genuinely happy when errors in your logic were pointed out because everyone benefits when they move together toward clearer understanding.

A dialogue process as described by Bohm is based on acknowledging and questioning assumptions.

Where did our beliefs come from and why are we so identified with them? Maybe we didn’t even come up with them. They might be our understanding (or misunderstanding) or someone else’s positions and arguments. Are these serving us today?

To explore this, people sit together in a small group with no agenda, no leader, and no specific goals. They’re not trying to be persuasive. They’re not agreeing or disagreeing with anything said. The group is simply considering what each opinion means, while suspending further judgments.

What is a judgment?

How much of your day would you say is spent evaluating others—what they wear, what they say, how they work?

To be clear, the judgments we’re talking about aren’t the basic predictions and categorizations that your brain seems to be making all the time.

We’re talking about conscious comparisons you make against what you think is normal or acceptable. We’re often looking to see how someone stacks up against where they “should” be. We regularly do the same to ourselves.

What Bohm proposed was that a group would temporarily suspend all of these stories they had about how things “should” be. Without their evaluations, they would have more space to just listen to each other.

They would be participating, together, in coming to a shared sense of meaning while still recognizing each of the distinct starting places and ideas among group members.

According to Bohm, this isn’t easy. People have to pay attention to even notice when a judgment or assumption is present. Then it takes willingness to participate in the dialogue process to leave that assumption to the side and keep listening.

Bohm readily acknowledged that this could be frustrating and may not work if conditions like trust within the group were lacking. It isn’t always going to be practical, but in the right circumstances, such a dialogue could be richly rewarding.

Many organizations are continuing similar types of dialogue work today. It’s happening online and in the real world. One major coalition of groups promoting these skills and spaces for richer conversations to happen is the Listen First Project, currently with over 550 member organizations.

item.title: A Cheat Sheet for Coping With Postpartum Anxiety
item.description:
Parenting

A Cheat Sheet for Coping With Postpartum Anxiety

Advice for postpartum anxiety, a common condition that's largely not discussed.

Posted November 12, 2026

Key points
  • Postpartum anxiety (PPA) is one of the most common and misunderstood challenges new mothers face.
  • PPA is not postpartum depression or psychosis.
  • Shortness of breath and frightening thoughts about the baby's safety are some signs of new mother anxiety.
Source: Angel4leon/Pixabay

Postpartum anxiety (PPA) is not postpartum depression or psychosis, as the Lindsay Clancy trial brought to light. Rather, postpartum anxiety is one of the most common and misunderstood conditions after childbirth, yet we don’t talk about it.

New mothers experience it to varying degrees. You could have constant worry, experience intrusive and frightening thoughts about the baby's safety, or exhibit excessive behaviors like checking the baby monitor every other second.

PPA is an element of what’s called “matrescence.” This refers to the holistic, developmental process of becoming a mother and includes hormonal, neurological, and emotional changes that you go through after your baby arrives. In some cases, this veritable metamorphosis can precipitate a sharp increase in anxiety in some new mothers that is underappreciated and has not been well explored in medicine.

Too many mothers have anxiety and feel misunderstood and, beyond that, feel isolated and alone. Katie Grant, a mother of one, had severe postpartum anxiety and wanted to make sure others didn’t have to suffer as she did.

She lived it and wanted to support new moms by relaying pointers and comforting reassurance in quick doses because, as she says, “you’ve only got 2 minutes and a baby on your hip!”

The beauty of The Postpartum Anxiety Cheat Sheet is that the pocket-sized book fits in your diaper bag or, yes, your pants pocket. I reached out to Grant to hear more about what she wants new moms to know.

Susan Newman: We are bombarded with images of the idyllic new mom, but reality can be so different. How can a new mom experiencing postpartum anxiety, or PPA, be realistic and not get swept up in the fantasy of new mom perfection?

Katie Grant: The first thing a new mom can do is acknowledge that she is experiencing PPA. Admit to yourself and your loved ones that you are having a hard time and need help, patience, and understanding. Then, stop comparing yourself to those photo-shopped, perfectly lit photos on your feeds. No one has it that easy, and everyone is struggling. They’re lying if they say they’re not.

I also recommend one of the “MOMtras” from my book. A MOMtra is a mantra to repeat to yourself or out loud to help shift your mindset and ease your worry in this very moment. One of my favorites is, “My thoughts are not me. I am not my thoughts. My brain is playing tricks on me, but I can win this game.”

SN: Who are the best people to talk to for the new mom experiencing anxiety?

KG: You need to talk to yourself and let it be OK that you are feeling anxious and off. Then, I would say your partner or best friend—there are cheat sheets for both of those relationships—since they are the ones spending the most time with you and can notice changes right away. You will find exactly what to text your best friend, for instance, so you don’t have to think about it too hard.

Professional help is always a solid option. Talk to a therapist, OB-GYN, or pediatrician, or call or text the PSI (Postpartum Support International) HelpLine at 1-800-944-4773. They can help you in the moment and direct you to the best resources for your situation.

SN: You explain what intrusive thoughts are in your book and how they are extremely common, yet most moms don’t admit having them for fear of being taken literally. What can we do to normalize that aspect of postpartum anxiety?

KG: Yes, intrusive thoughts are one of the most common symptoms of PPA, but because they appear only in our mind, we are afraid people might think we want to act on them. Intrusive thoughts usually involve picturing harm coming to your baby. For me, it was picturing knives coming at my baby’s bald head. And, turns out, that exact image is the most common. That helped me understand that I did indeed have PPA when I saw that on a list of screening questions.

What we can do to normalize this aspect is to make it widely known that PPA happens to most, or at least many, mothers. Those thoughts do not mean you want to or will act on them. They are your brain showing up in protective overdrive so you can and will shield your baby from harm. It is your mother instinct stuck in the "on" position. Admitting those thoughts to your doctor or a trusted loved one can help put that switch back into the "off" position.

SN: You have a dozen cheat sheets, short lists with directions, to help moms better understand their anxiety. In “Cheat Sheet #10,” you ask (and answer) how you know if the situation is really an emergency; “Cheat Sheet #11” addresses how to explain what seems like your odd behavior to your baby’s older sibling; and “Cheat Sheet #8” goes into how to ask for help when you need it, to name a few. Which ones do you feel are the most important for anxious mothers?

KG: I would say the most asked for would be “Cheat Sheet #1 For Your Partner.” It is imperative that your partner recognizes what you’re going through, how they can help you, and how to find professional help for you. Your partner doesn’t get to decide when you should be better. Partners need to be educated about this condition and be there for you, not against you.

Source: Katie Grant

“Cheat Sheet #5 For Your Pediatrician” flips the narrative about baby wellness checkups expressly to focus on your anxiety. Pediatricians are the doctors who see you most often after you have a baby, and they should be trained in what to look for, but most of them are not. They are not supposed to focus solely on the baby, even if that’s what their title says. If you know what to mention and the right questions to ask, you’ll be able to help your pediatrician help you.

Learn from quick tips and get the support you need

Whether you call it a cheat sheet, checklist, or guide, The Postpartum Anxiety Cheat Sheet can get you through the times you doubt yourself and lead you to the support you need. It can also help you figure out if what you are feeling is “OK” as you pace the floor with a baby you can’t seem to put down.

When you feel overwhelmed by anxiety, heeding the factoids in this useful little book and urging loved ones to do the same can make a huge difference in the often rocky, anxiety-driven transition to motherhood that is PPA, postpartum anxiety.

item.title: Marsha Linehan’s Bold Legacy Extends Far Beyond DBT
item.description:
Borderline Personality Disorder

Marsha Linehan’s Bold Legacy Extends Far Beyond DBT

Linehan is a role model for a social science that truly values lived experience.

Posted November 12, 2026

Key points
  • Marsha Linehan, creator of dialectical behavior therapy, passed away in Seattle last week.
  • Marsha embraced lived experience to inform her groundbreaking scientific and clinical work.
  • Her bold legacy extends far beyond DBT to challenging sexism and stigma in social science.

This post was written with input from Ursula Whiteside, Ph.D., a former student of Marsha Linehan.

Earlier this week, the field lost an icon. Marsha Linehan, creator of dialectical behavior therapy, passed away in Seattle on November 10. She was 83.

Marsha earned her Ph.D. in experimental psychology from Loyola University and received her clinical training as a postdoctoral fellow at Stony Brook University. She then embarked on a storied clinical and academic career at the University of Washington, starting in 1977.

Most of the world knows Marsha the scientist. Some of us were lucky enough to know Marsha the person. One of my great career fortunes was to join the University of Washington faculty in 2000, where I got to know both.

Marsha was a true trailblazer. She formulated DBT, a treatment that’s helped thousands of people live more satisfying lives, during an era when women held little power in the social sciences. Marsha’s formidable personality, clinical acumen, and advanced training in experimental psychology and behavior modification all contributed to her success in creating DBT. None of these traits would have been sufficient, however, without her lived experience. Those of us who collaborated on Marsha’s research projects and attended her clinical teams saw this every day.

Marsha suffered from symptoms of the very condition she created DBT to treat. She knew, through subjective experience, the life challenges and acute despair that so often accompany mental health struggles. After ascending through the ranks of academia and establishing herself as an exemplary social scientist, Marsha described her mental illness in a 2011 New York Times article.

It’s nearly impossible to convey just how bold Marsha’s decision to reveal her personal experiences with mental illness was. As many of us know, revealing one’s own mental health issues is almost always disqualifying for careers in academia. Marsha herself waited 25 years after her first writings on DBT to do so.

Had Marsha come out before or during graduate school, or before she was an established leader in the field, her career would likely have ended before it began. Marsha, like so many of us, hid her mental illness for decades because it was necessary to be taken seriously in a field that stigmatizes and marginalizes its own. As I've discussed elsewhere, little has changed in this regard in the 15 years since Marsha came out.

In honoring Marsha’s legacy, those of us in the field should take a hard look in the mirror. Without Marsha’s lived experience informing her treatment development, the world would be without DBT, which has helped tens of thousands of adults and adolescents and saved many lives.

Do we really value lived experience, or do we acknowledge it performatively? Are we still writing off and marginalizing the subjective views of those with mental illness—whether inside or outside the field? Do we, through acts big and small, discourage or even prevent those with lived experience from becoming the deeply caring, transformative clinicians Marsha so boldly embodied?

A common refrain in the helping professions is that we’re not defined by our mental illness. The sentiment behind these statements is almost always sincere, and surely we’re not fully defined by our foibles or frailties. Yet if stigma were eradicated—something Marsha championed—there would be no need for such statements. We could embrace our mental illness, not reject it. These traits would be mere parts of us, not our foibles or frailties.

When a field devoted to treating mental illness marginalizes those who experience it, we promote stigma and shame from the very top. The message to individuals is to reject being defined by core, enduring parts ourselves. We reinforce negative views of mental illness within our ranks and among the public, and we promote and internalize shame. Although our intentions are just the opposite, we stigmatize yet again.

Marsha taught us another way. Let’s honor her bold legacy by carrying her life's work forward.

item.title: Animal Play: From the Trash Can to Theories of Fairness
item.description:
Animal Behavior

Animal Play: From the Trash Can to Theories of Fairness

Play in animals was once wrongly thought to be a useless behavior.

Posted November 12, 2026

Key points
  • Discarding play as a useless behavior with no purpose at all proved to be an egregious mistake.
  • Social play is based on a foundation of fairness, perhaps a uniquely egalitarian behavior.
  • Play is important in adopting dog; shelter dogs who don’t play with objects are less likely to be adopted.
Source: Rebecca Niemiec/with permission

I’ve been nose-deep in dog play for more than 50 years, and I never get bored. Dogs, like other animals, just want to have fun without a care in the world. These are some of my field notes from watching three dogs at play—Jethro, a large German shepherd/rottweiler/hound mutt; Zeke, a black lab; and Suki, a Belgian sheepdog:

Jethro runs toward Zeke, stops immediately in front of him, crouches on his forelimbs, wags his tail, barks, and immediately lunges, biting Zeke’s scruff and shaking his head rapidly from side to side. Jethro works his way around to his backside and mounts him, jumps off, does a rapid bow, lunges at his side and slams him with his hips, leaps up and bites his neck, and runs away. Zeke takes off in wild pursuit of Jethro, leaps on his back and bites his muzzle and scruff, then shakes his head rapidly from side to side. Suki bounds in and chases Jethro and Zeke, and they all wrestle with one another. They part for a few minutes, sniffing here and there and resting. Then Jethro walks over to Zeke, extends his paw toward Zeke’s head, and nips at his ears. Zeke gets up and jumps on Jethro’s back, bites him, and grasps him around his waist. They then fall to the ground and mouth wrestle. They chase and then roll over and play. Suki decides to jump in, and all three frolic until they’re exhausted.

Play is fun and serious business

For an ethologist, play is a behavior to take seriously, and it's also serious business for animals at play. Yet when I first started studying play decades ago, a number of my colleagues didn’t think so. They thought play should be tossed into a “wastebasket” because there wasn't any obvious goal or function.

On the surface, many people thought that play serves no obvious purpose. Very few people think that today. Play is improvisational and mixes a hodgepodge of behaviors from other contexts, like fighting, mating, hunting, self-defense, and so on. Dogs might growl, bite, hump, and chase in quick succession, and they might exaggerate, minimize, and interrupt these behaviors. After growling fiercely, they might bite softly, and after mounting and starting to hump, they might abruptly quit and take turns chasing. These behaviors are a kaleidoscope of the senses that helps to define play.

That’s a lot to get out of watching animals goof off and zoom around. But that’s what can happen when you observe animals closely and think carefully about what they do and why. Since play is defined by joy, it’s valid to ask: Why did play evolve—what is it good for? How do we define and recognize it? And how does it help animals survive?

After decades of studying play, I’ve learned that play is very important, and my research has led to a series of wide-ranging questions. These include: How do animals communicate that they’re playing and not doing something else, like fighting or mating? How do animals play? Does play require certain agreements to ensure cooperation, trust, and reciprocity, as well as to repair trust—such as apologizing—if something goes wrong? If so, does that mean animals have a basic sense of justice or morality? And if that’s true, then is morality an evolved trait? Does “being fair” mean being more fit in evolutionary terms? In other words, do nice guys, gals, and their genes last longest? Do the friendliest and nicest individuals survive best?

What is play, and why is it important?

Social play is almost like school for nonhuman animals, and it's not just for fun. Play helps individuals within the group to get along, since play relies on and teaches trust, cooperation, niceness, fairness, forgiveness, and humility. Meticulous studies have shown that play fosters physical development and motor skills, it provides critical socialization, it helps develop physical life skills (like hunting and self-defense), and it develops the mind, in part by allowing animals to train for unexpected situations. Play feeds brain, body, and community, teaching young animals what they will need to do to survive in the world as well as the interpersonal skills to thrive in their own society. Play is also an important consideration for dogs that are adopted. In the United States, shelter dogs who don’t choose to play with objects are less likely to be adopted.

Play begins with a bow

For a model of fair play, let’s go to the dogs. Dogs signal social play using the “play bow.” This is what Jethro does first in my field notes above: He crouches on his forelegs, his hindlegs straight and his tail wagging. With or without barking, this is how dogs say, “I want to play with you!”

The dog on the right bows to ask his friend to play with him.
Source: Marc Bekoff

The play bow both initiates play and keeps it going if there’s a break. It’s used whenever something happens that might end play. For instance, if a dog is about to do something, or just did something, that might be misinterpreted—like growling viciously and biting—the play bow says, I’m going to bite you, but it’s only in play. Or, I didn’t mean to bite so hard; let’s keep playing. So, if you don’t want to play, don’t bow.

The golden rules of play: Fairness matters

Uncooperative play is an oxymoron. When cooperation and fairness break down, play not only stops, but it also becomes impossible. In essence, animal play appears to rely on the universal human value of the Golden Rule: Do unto others as you would have them do unto you. I summarize this as “the four golden rules of play”: (1) Ask first and communicate clearly; (2) Mind your manners; (3) Admit when you are wrong; (4) Be honest.

Coda

All in all, social play is based on a foundation of fairness, perhaps a uniquely egalitarian behavior. If we define morality as a set of social rules and expectations that neutralize differences among individuals in an effort to maintain group harmony, then that’s exactly what we find in animals when they play.

I’ve truly enjoyed watching how different patterns of animal play went from being discarded as a “wastebasket” of useless information to playing a key role in the development of ideas and theories about the evolution and development of animal morality—wild justice, as Jessica Pierce and I call it—and finding a home in areas such as human development and business ethics. And what's really exciting is that there is room for much more research on animals who frenetically zoom around here and there without a care in the world.

item.title: Quieting Food Noise in Children
item.description:
Parenting

Quieting Food Noise in Children

Does your child think about food all the time? Parents can help quiet the noise.

Posted November 12, 2026

Key points
  • Kids can experience food noise, just like adults, but parents can help quiet the noise.
  • Setting up a structure around meals and eating lets children get in touch with their hunger.
  • When adults don't control how much children are eating, they're better able to listen to their hunger.

Does your child seem to think about food all the time? You may find that they often ask when the next snack is, worry about whether they will get enough of a favorite food, sneak or hide food, or seem really focused on foods they often don’t get. Sometimes this is called food noise. Food noise is when a child finds themselves thinking about food a lot, even when they aren’t physically hungry. Many of us adults experience this as well, so we can relate to how our children feel and understand that it can be hard to reduce these thoughts.

As parents, our first reaction may be to set more limits. We may find ourselves hiding certain foods, locking cabinets, controlling portions, telling our child when they have had enough, or encouraging them to choose a “healthier” option. These responses come from a good place because we want our children to develop healthy eating habits in the long term. But sometimes, this control causes the food noise to get even louder.

A few strategies to help quiet this noise involve creating an environment around structure, trust, and food neutrality.

Start by Adding Structure to Meals and Snacks

Kids do well when they know what to expect, and eating is no different. A regular meal and snack routine reassures children that another opportunity to eat is coming.

We recommend three meals and one to two planned snacks each day. Younger children might need an extra snack. The exact times will depend on school, activities, family schedules, and your child’s needs. Having this predictable routine helps children learn:

  • They will have another opportunity to eat.
  • They don’t need to worry when food is coming.
  • There will be enough food for them.

Posting the schedule for everyone to see in a centralized area, like on the pantry door or fridge, can be a good reminder.

If your child asks for food shortly after a meal or you catch them sneaking food at an unscheduled time, your role is to redirect them. Instead of saying, “You just ate! There is no way you can be hungry,” you might say:

  • “I hear you. Snack time is coming. Let’s see what time we’re having it today.”
  • “Let’s check the schedule and see when snack time is.”
  • “Let’s save that for your next snack time.”

Trust Kids to Listen to Their Bodies

Babies are born knowing how much they need to eat. They stop when they are full by pushing the bottle away and have telltale signs when they are hungry. Somewhere along the way, many kids stop listening to those hunger and fullness signals and begin relying on their parents and caregivers to decide how much they need.

This might look like encouraging them to take two more bites or finish everything on their plate and restricting how much they eat of more desirable foods when we feel like they are eating too much. This double-sided pressure often leads to children losing some of their ability to self-regulate their eating, which in turn leads to undereating or overeating at times.

Kids who become out of touch with these cues often have more food noise. When food feels scarce, they want it more. We encourage parents to let their children decide whether and how much they want to eat from what is provided at meals and snacks. When it becomes age-appropriate, we encourage children to make their own plates at meals. Parents can still serve hot foods if needed and ask the child how much they would like on their plate. This is not saying that they can eat as much as they want, whenever they want it. Not at all! It is saying that at the scheduled eating times, we want parents to step back and let kids take the lead in deciding how much they need to eat because only they know how hungry they are when they come to an eating time. Just like you and just like me.

At first, when children have this control, you may find that they will overeat. This is totally normal. They are learning, and it can take time for them to begin regulating on their own again. The important thing is to trust the process and keep practicing.

Take Some of the Power Away From Food

We often put foods into categories: good or bad, healthy or unhealthy. Kids pick up on these labels. When certain foods are placed on pedestals and others are treated as foods to avoid, it can have the opposite effect we intend. Kids become less interested in the food we call “healthy” and more interested in the foods we call "bad."

The same happens when certain foods are tightly restricted. When cookies are tightly controlled at home, they may start to feel like these amazing, special things they can never quite get their hands on. And because these treats seem so special or hard to get, kids will often focus on them even more when they are available.

Taking some of the power away from these foods does not mean cookies need to be available all day or that your child decides what is served at every meal. It means providing some structure while keeping the way we talk about food simple, neutral, and positive.

Food talk might sound like:

  • “We eat some foods every day and others once in a while.”
  • “Our bodies need many different foods to grow and learn.”
  • “Some foods give us quick energy, while others help us stay full longer.”

The take-home here is to avoid labeling food for yourself and when talking to your child. Kids are always listening to how we talk about food. Modeling simple, neutral food language helps them learn to see food without judgment or guilt.

Quieting food noise isn’t about teaching children to think less about food. It’s about creating an environment where they don’t have to think about it so much.

item.title: Mental Health Care Has a Time Problem
item.description:
Therapy

Mental Health Care Has a Time Problem

We tell people to make time for mental health. What if we've got it backward?

Posted November 12, 2026

Key points
  • Nearly half of untreated adults who felt they needed mental health care said they didn't have the time for it.
  • Research suggests that certain well-being practices lasting 30 seconds or less can improve mental health.
  • Across a range of well-being practices, practicing more often—not longer—is associated with better outcomes.
  • We need both policies to protect time for treatment and practices that fit into the moments we already have.
Source: SHVETS production/Pexels

We tell people to make time for their mental health as if time were theirs to make.

For someone paid by the hour, a therapy appointment can cost wages as well as a copay. For a parent or caregiver, getting help may require arranging care for someone else first. Even when treatment is technically available, it may not be available when we can actually use it.

The World Health Organization is asking that people’s lived experiences shape mental health services. We could start by taking seriously an experience that is easy to mistake for an excuse: “I don’t have time.”

The latest National Survey on Drug Use and Health, released in July, found that 49.1 percent of American adults with mental illness received no mental health treatment in 2025. Among untreated adults who felt they needed care, 48.3 percent said they did not have enough time. Cost was an even more common barrier (61.4 percent).

We need policies that protect time for mental health care. But what are people supposed to do while those protections remain out of reach, or when care isn’t available?

My interest in that question began at Plum Village, a mindfulness practice center founded by Thích Nhất Hạnh. During a stay there, I proudly told a monk named Brother Treasure that I’d just meditated for three hours.

He smiled, “How about three breaths? That’s all that you need to tune into the present moment.”

I was so embarrassed. But that exchange helped shape my research as a psychologist: What if well-being didn’t have to compete with the rest of our lives for time?

At Berkeley, my colleagues and I studied an exercise called self-compassionate touch: resting your hands over your heart and belly while responding to yourself with a kind inner voice. We randomly assigned 135 college students to practice either this exercise or a finger-tapping control group for 20 seconds a day for a month.

Compared to daily finger-tapping, just 20 seconds a day of self-compassionate touch was associated with greater improvements in self-compassion, stress, and mental health. The effects were comparable in size to those found in much more time-intensive interventions.

I call practices like these micropractices. They take 30 seconds or less, or can be woven into something you’re already doing. Noticing your footsteps on the way to the bus. Taking three slow, deep breaths before opening your inbox. Doing a yoga pose between tasks.

Although we extended this research on 20-second self-compassionate touch in a six-month study of 497 U.S. adults, published last month, my research alone can’t tell us how broadly this idea applies. But as I started looking beyond my own research, I found further evidence that practices can have measurable effects in seconds. In a separate experiment, another research group found that 20 seconds of self-soothing touch reduced the stress hormone cortisol following a stressful experience. And recent studies show that 30 seconds of slow, deep breathing can reduce anxiety, slow heart rate, and increase alpha and theta brain-wave activity associated with calm and focused attention.

More broadly, I kept running into studies that challenged an assumption I had largely taken for granted: that more time means more benefit.

An analysis of 203 randomized controlled trials on meditation found duration of sessions wasn’t associated with better mental health outcomes.

A study of 21,088 mindfulness app users objectively tracked session duration and frequency. The pattern was similar: Consistent practice was associated with reduced stress; longer sessions were not.

And it’s not just meditation. In an analysis of 137 trials of touch interventions and practices involving 12,966 people, more sessions were associated with better mental health outcomes. But longer sessions? No extra benefit. In fact, when it came to lowering cortisol, and even reducing blood pressure, longer sessions were less effective than shorter ones.

Breathwork points in the same direction. An analysis of 12 randomized controlled trials of breathwork interventions (like slow deep breathing) totaling 785 adults found that reductions in stress were not associated with session length.

And sometimes, breaking the same amount of movement into smaller pieces can be more beneficial than doing it all at once. In one study, six five-minute walks spread across the day improved mood, fatigue, and food cravings more than a single 30-minute walk.

None of this means that 30 seconds is always enough, or that longer practices have no value. But many of us only have a 30-second window—or at least a lot more of them: between Zoom meetings, in the checkout line, at a red light, or while waiting for the microwave to ring. And if the choice is between 30 seconds and nothing at all, I’d bet on 30 seconds.

The point is not that complex suffering has a 30-second solution. Nor is this a substitute for psychotherapy, medication, or any longer practice that is already helping. It’s more like brushing your teeth: It doesn’t replace the dentist, but it helps you keep things in check. In the same way, these tiny practices can give you a way of not being left empty-handed when the system isn’t there.

Lack of time, however, isn’t merely a personal problem.

A 2024 study found that after states adopted paid-sick-leave mandates, Medicaid-financed prescriptions for mental health conditions increased by about 6 percent per year. Protecting people’s time can help them use care. And we can also design forms of support that demand less of that time. These aren’t competing approaches. We need both.

Institutions need to do more than tell us to take care of ourselves. A company that offers employees a breathing exercise should protect time to attend a therapy appointment. A health system that offers a self-guided resource should provide a clear route to a clinician.

The best self-help doesn’t teach people that they should be able to handle everything themselves. It creates more moments in which help is possible while leaving the door open to more.

We need to move beyond reminding people that their mental health matters. We need to take “I don’t have time” seriously. People deserve care that fits the lives they actually have. Sometimes that means systems that protect an hour for therapy. Sometimes it means discovering that a meaningful practice doesn’t require another hour, or even another minute.

It can begin with 30 seconds you already have.

item.title: Maladaptive Daydreaming and ADHD
item.description:
ADHD

Maladaptive Daydreaming and ADHD

Is your fantasy life more engaging than the real thing?

Posted November 12, 2026

Key points
  • Fantasy that replaces real life is not a formal diagnosis, yet it is especially common in people with ADHD.
  • Analysis of Reddit posts shows fantasies of a perfect self and companions who always offer support.
  • Low self-esteem is common in ADHD, and fantasy may offer a refuge from years of rejection and criticism.

One of the greatest things about the internet is finding out you’re not alone. I feel sorry for those Victorian souls who had a weird thought and simply had to live with it. Instead of going on Reddit and searching, “Does anyone else pretend to be a chicken to get to sleep at night?” they sat there in their little nightcaps by candlelight, feeling like the biggest weirdos on Earth, when they could have been doomscrolling for three hours about how many people had the exact same fantasy and, even more comforting, even weirder and more bizarre ones. Which brings me to my most recent discovery. It not only made me feel less of an oddball, but it also gave me that now-familiar feeling: Has anyone on this planet ever had a truly unique experience?

According to subreddit threads, no. We are all infinitely bizarre and confused creatures, bumbling around and trying to look like we’ve got our sh*t together when we clearly don’t. That brings me a great deal of comfort, knowing I’m not alone.

As a woman with ADHD, I’ve spent my life feeling like an alien who has landed on Earth while everyone else received the manual on how to be human except me. It turns out that even that alien feeling is common among people with ADHD. Through my research into women with ADHD, I keep finding stories I thought were as odd and unique as that chicken dream, only to discover they’re not.

One of the most shameful aspects of ADHD for many of us is how much of our mental landscape is taken up by living in entirely fictional versions of our lives. Some of these are so vivid that they intermingle with reality, and it becomes hard to tell the real life from the fantasy. This might seem like a very strange concept to a neurotypical person, but many ADHDers will resonate with it on several levels. I used to do it so much that I truly didn’t realise it was a thing. I thought everyone lived in a parallel universe of epic proportions.

This is known as maladaptive daydreaming (MD), a proposed condition in which someone gets absorbed in vivid, story-like fantasy for so long that it takes over their life. The term was coined in 2002 by Eli Somer of the University of Haifa, who described it as extensive fantasy activity that replaces human interaction or interferes with academic, interpersonal, or vocational functioning (Somer, 2002). The fantasies usually have characters, plots, and settings, and people with MD can tell their fantasies aren’t real, which separates it from psychosis. It isn’t an official diagnosis, but as researchers like myself uncover more about the lived experiences of people with ADHD, it appears to be especially common in this population (Somer et al., 2017; Theodor-Katz et al., 2022).

What is it about ADHD that makes maladaptive daydreaming so appealing? From my own anecdotal research, it can be a form of escape from a world that often feels unkind and full of rejection. From early childhood, many people with ADHD experience increased levels of bullying and negative feedback because of their behaviour (Abregú-Crespo et al., 2024; Becker et al., 2017), which can create deeply felt low self-esteem and a sense of unworthiness. One way of coping can be to escape into a fantasy of “One day…I’ll show them all!”

There is something about the ADHD mind that tends to wander off into other dimensions, but when it does, what are the most common fantasies people engage in? Getting people to open up about the innermost workings of their minds is notoriously difficult, even in non-judgmental research settings, but a quick subreddit search throws up some revealing insights. Nowacki and Pyszkowska (2024) found that Reddit users described fantasies about being a perfect version of themselves, undoing past mistakes, and having imagined companions who offer constant support. Others imagined being a confident leader, the opposite of their real-life selves, or went back to painful memories to have their younger selves rescued. One poster dated the start of their excessive daydreaming to being bullied by siblings. While these accounts are not specific to ADHD, they show how fantasy can serve as both comfort and escape from a world that feels unforgiving.

So if your mind is off in another universe right now, don’t beat yourself up. You’re in very good company, and with a little kindness you can enjoy the daydreams without letting them run the show. In my book of ADHD hacks, How to Get Your Sh*t Together, I devote a whole chapter to forgiving yourself and all your ADHD quirks, and daydreaming is just one of them (Murphy, [2026]).

item.title: Dog-ma: Jung, Synchronicity, and the Beach Yoga Class That Was Ruff
item.description:
Synchronicity

Dog-ma: Jung, Synchronicity, and the Beach Yoga Class That Was Ruff

Meaning sometimes arrives through timing rather than through explanation.

Posted November 12, 2026

Key points
  • Synchronicity is Jung’s meaningful coincidence, like a dog fighting its leash mid-meditation.
  • Meaning-making comes from noticing the happening, not the coincidence itself.
  • Noticing these moments brings more optimism.
Not just a dog on a beach
Source: Diogo Miranda / Pexels

I sat cross-legged in the sand, doing my best impression of someone with their thoughts under control, when the yoga instructor said the line every meditator has heard a thousand times: Your mind is like a puppy. It wanders off; you gently bring it back. It wanders off again; you bring it back again. No yelling. No drama. Just patient redirection, over and over, forever, amen.

And at that exact moment—not as a vague afterthought, but right then—a woman 20 feet away in front of the class, behind the instructor, and in front of the ocean, was locked in a full-contact wrestling match with an actual dog on an actual leash. Pulling. Tugging. The dog wanted the water, she wanted the boardwalk, and neither of them was interested in gentle redirection. It was the least zen scene on the entire beach, unfolding in real time as a soundtrack to a lecture about zen.

I opened one eye. I am fairly sure I laughed out loud, which is not great yoga etiquette.

Here's the thing about moments like that: You can shrug them off as a coincidence or let them stop you in your tracks. I let this one stop me, because it did something a metaphor alone never quite manages—it made the metaphor physical. I didn't just hear that my mind is like a puppy. I watched a mind-sized puppy misbehave in real time, a very short distance from where I sat trying to master mine.

Carl Jung had a word for this—synchronicity—meaningful coincidences that seem to carry significance beyond ordinary cause and effect. Jung wasn't claiming the universe is a puppeteer pulling strings so your yoga class gets better sound effects. He was pointing at something subtler: that meaning sometimes arrives sideways, through timing, rather than head-on, through explanation.

For decades, that idea lived mostly in Jungian circles, treated as a little too mystical for serious psychology to touch. But it turns out some very serious psychologists have been touching it anyway. Pninit Russo-Netzer and Tamar Icekson, researchers who study meaning and well-being, spent years interviewing people about their synchronicity experiences—the goosebump moments, the "You would not believe what just happened" moments—and out of those interviews they built something researchers love and mystics tend to distrust: a model.

Receptiveness, an Exceptional Encounter, and Meaning-Detecting

They call it REM, and no, it has nothing to do with sleep. It stands for: Receptiveness—being open, attentive, quietly available to what's happening around you (which, not coincidentally, is exactly what a beach at sunrise with your eyes half-closed is designed to produce). Then an Exceptional encounter—the unexpected event that rhymes with something already stirring inside you. And finally, Meaning-detecting—the moment you consciously connect the two and let it mean something.

Notice that meaning-detecting is a verb, not a lightning bolt. The dog and the puppy metaphor didn't hand me a revelation. I had to reach out and pick it up. Russo-Netzer and Icekson later built a whole scale around this—the Synchronicity Awareness and Meaning-Detecting Scale—and their data suggests something wonderfully unmystical: People who notice these moments and let them land tend to report more optimism, a stronger sense that life holds together, and higher life satisfaction. Not because coincidences are magic, but because noticing them is a skill, and it's a skill that keeps paying you back.

Which brings me to the dog, one more time. The woman eventually won. Or the dog decided the fight wasn't worth it; it's hard to say who negotiated whom. But watching it, I thought: That's what my brain does to me on a slow Wednesday when a worry won't drop the leash. And what the instructor was really teaching wasn't a metaphor about puppies at all. It was a rehearsal for exactly that moment on the beach—so that when my own mind starts pulling toward the water, I remember I'm allowed to just...turn, and walk, and not make it a fight.

I don't think the universe scheduled that dog for my benefit. I think the universe is simply generous with material, all the time, and most of it goes right past us because we're not receptive enough to catch it. That morning, for once, I paid just enough attention to catch the pitch. The dog never did learn to heel. Neither, most mornings, have I. But I’m a tad more hopeful.

item.title: The In Real Life Act: The Antidote to Loneliness
item.description:
Loneliness

The In Real Life Act: The Antidote to Loneliness

Friendship is becoming matched and sold; public places offer something different.

Posted November 12, 2026

Key points
  • People are increasingly using paid friend-matching apps.
  • Public places offer repeated, unchosen encounters that can build trust across differences.
  • Investing in shared places, from parks to soccer fields at transit stations, help connection reach everyone.

For the last three years, my husband has headed off to our local park most Sundays. Braving the sweltering Texas summers and occasional winter frost, he is joined by an impromptu group of fellow players from different countries, jobs, ages, and backgrounds. The seeming sacredness of this act may come from a shared love of soccer, or fútbol, but what I see as most magnificent is the emergent nature of the collective. There is no sign-up or group text; whoever arrives plays. The group trusts people will turn out, and whatever that looks like will work.

A few hundred feet away, my daughter does something similar on the playground. I imagined when she was a baby that we could meet up with other families there, and sometimes we do, but more often we trust in the shared experience of whatever the park provides. This serendipity depends on a space that holds it.

Loneliness Isn’t a Personal Problem

In May 2021, Julianne Holt-Lunstad and I wrote about the power of place—how designing places to be inclusive of all ages, reconnect us with nature, and provide a welcoming space and a reason to connect with others—foundational structures in combating loneliness and fostering social health. This is something that the U.S. Surgeon General’s Advisory on Social Connection calls a part of social infrastructure. These relatively modest investments in social infrastructure can advance long-term human connection.

In the absence of these resources, people with the means are increasingly paying to fulfill their social needs. This trend is part of a long lineage of proposed solutions that treat loneliness as a personal problem. But addressing loneliness is inherently a collective challenge requiring collective action.

This fall, U.S. Senator Chris Murphy (D-Conn) proposed a way to fund this collective need: the In Real Life (IRL) Act. The IRL Act would create a tax on social media platforms that make at least $500 million in ad revenue and use those dollars to create a Social Capital Fund. This fund would flow directly to cities, towns, and tribes to support places that foster social ties, such as parks, libraries, and community spaces, and the groups and programs that keep these places filled with life.

A Shared Space, Not a Shared App

No algorithms would have matched those soccer players; it required a shared space, not a shared app. This makes those connections more valuable, not less; in a study of more than 70 million U.S. Facebook users, friendships across economic lines were among the strongest predictors of upward mobility. And Trust for Public Land found that nearly two-thirds of Americans had a positive conversation with a stranger in an outdoor public space over the past year. These shared spaces become exponentially stronger when they are combined with inclusive programming.

What This Could Look Like

StationSoccer in Atlanta, Georgia, offers a glimpse at the benefits this type of support from the proposed Social Capital Fund might offer. Putting soccer fields at Atlanta-regional transit stations, StationSoccer is a program of the nonprofit Soccer in the Streets partnered with the City of Atlanta, their transit agency (MARTA), Atlanta United Community Fund, Georgia Power, and Children’s Healthcare of Atlanta.

What started as an idea to activate a single dead space quickly burgeoned into a vibrant citywide connective movement, and just recently garnered an honorable mention in the Fast Company Innovation by Design Awards.

Part of what makes this program so successful is that it meets the needs for supportive design: It is inherently accessible and inclusive because it sits where commuters and neighbors already travel, it gets kids and their families outdoors, and its programming keeps them coming back. Taking once underused land and transforming it into well-used social infrastructure has likely strengthened the social capital of thousands of Atlanta children and their families. Programs like these show what becomes possible when connection is funded collectively, rather than left to those who can afford to pay for it.

What we choose to invest in at every scale—as individuals, neighborhoods, and nations—creates the shape of the worlds we inhabit. May we choose to invest in real-life serendipity and the spaces that hold it.

item.title: Why Smart People Still Believe These 5 Myths
item.description:
Intelligence

Why Smart People Still Believe These 5 Myths

Intelligence won’t protect you from these myths. Even scientists get fooled.

Posted November 12, 2026

Key points
  • IQ offers slim protection from false beliefs because rational thinking is different from intelligence.
  • Ideas about rewards, passion, grit, practice, and mindset rest on weaker evidence than their fame suggests.
  • Rewards don't automatically destroy motivation as incentives and enjoyment work together, not in opposition.
Source: Google Gemini/AI image generator

Chances are, you will succumb to at least one common seasonal false belief. When you see a child queued up to see Santa having a full-blown meltdown, do you suspect excessive candy cane consumption? Maybe you insist that family members wear winter beanies because you believe most body heat escapes from the head? Have you moved a poinsettia out of a toddler's reach for fear of poisoning? If so, you are in great company, but also 100% wrong, according to science!

A dozen controlled trials show that sugar does not cause hyperactivity, the head accounts for only about 10 percent of body heat loss, and poinsettias pose no serious poisoning risks (Vreeman & Carroll, 2008). Despite what you might believe, each statement above is refuted by scientific evidence.

As I stated in my last post on popular psychology myths, the reasons why "smart" people reject facts are voluminous, but often include cultural and personal experience, inability or unwillingness to examine evidence, and herd mentality (whereby group endorsement supports believability). People also resist abandoning false beliefs when they perceive no compelling reason to change or fail to recognize the consequences of those beliefs. To fully understand how beliefs influence behavior, we must first distinguish beliefs that science can refute from those that cannot be objectively dispelled. For example, we won't debate things like how much sex is appropriate in a marriage, how much money should be contributed to charities, or whether stealing is acceptable if you are starving. Science cannot answer these types of questions. Instead, below I identify popular myths that hinder organizational performance, thinking, and decision-making, focusing primarily on motivation and achievement. I close by emphasizing that scientific understanding must remain open to revision as new evidence emerges, reflecting the evolving nature of research.

1. Rewards kill intrinsic motivation

Generations of parents and educators have been conditioned to believe that offering rewards undermines the joy of doing something for its own sake. The myth suggests that paying a child to read means raising a child who never reads for fun again. The evidence tells a different story. The detrimental effects of rewards are narrow and occur only under specific conditions (Hoffman, 2025).

A 40-year meta-analysis revealed intrinsic motivation (i.e., doing things voluntarily and for pleasure) and extrinsic rewards (e.g., recognition, money, or praise) jointly predict performance, with internal drive better predicting work quality and incentives better predicting work quantity (Cerasoli et al., 2014). As I argued in The Paradox of Passion, the brain does not sort motivation into tidy "intrinsic" and "extrinsic" buckets. Rewards, whether a paycheck, praise, or a dopamine rush, covertly shape almost everything we choose to do (Hoffman, 2025). The question is not whether to use rewards, but how to use them productively.

2. Find passion and bliss follows

"Follow your passion" is a motivational speaker's mantra and the foundational message in many commencement speeches. The advice implies that passion is discoverable, like buried treasure, and that finding it is the secret to a fulfilling life.

Research suggests this belief can backfire.

People who view interests as fixed and discoverable are less curious about topics outside existing interests, expect newfound passion to provide limitless motivation, and lose interest faster when work gets difficult (O'Keefe et al., 2018). In reality, passion is more often developed than discovered. It typically follows competence, effort, investment, and reward rather than preceding them (Hoffman, 2025). Waiting for passion to strike is a reliable way to wait a very long time.

3. Grit determines success

Few constructs have moved from a journal to the bestseller list to school policy as quickly as “grit,” defined as passion and perseverance for long-term goals.

A meta-analysis of 88 independent samples representing 66,807 individuals found that grit's relationship with performance is modest, that it overlaps heavily with the established trait of conscientiousness, and that perseverance is what really drives long-term success (Credé et al., 2017). Persistence matters, but grit is neither new nor the secret sauce it has been marketed to be. Labeling a struggling student as "lacking grit" repackages the old claim that some people are simply unmotivated (Hoffman, 2017), using a memorable and emotionally charged term that describes someone who overcomes obstacles.

4. Practice makes perfect

The "10,000-hour rule" suggests that intentional and sufficient practice will turn you into a bona fide expert. Talent, in this view, is optional. A meta-analysis of deliberate practice studies shows us otherwise. Dedicated practice explained about 26% of performance differences in games, 21% in music, 18% in sports, 4% in education, and less than 1% in professions (Macnamara et al., 2014). Practice is essential, but not a guarantee of expertise. Perfect practice is far different than engagement alone. Skills can be developed, but objective feedback, strategy changes, and openness to criticism also matter.

5. Mindset transforms academic achievement

Believing that intelligence is fixed can limit intellectual growth. After all, if you think you cannot change, why try? For decades, the antidote to fixed intelligence was a brief growth mindset intervention, often a single session designed to persuade believers that neuroplasticity means the brain can grow. This myth permeates schools as the magic solution to academic apathy. However, a meta-analysis of 63 studies with 97,672 participants found little effect of mindset training on actual achievement. Ironically, studies conducted by authors who received financial benefits from mindset consulting reported more positive findings than those without incentives (Macnamara & Burgoyne, 2023). Believing you can change is important, but a brief training session from a mindset coach is no better a solution to academic achievement than watching an infomercial and expecting to look 20 years younger by using some random face cream.

Do you harbor any of these false beliefs?

The most likely answer is “YES,” and according to research, you will continue to embrace your beliefs despite the evidence presented here. If it is any consolation, scientists are not immune to harboring false beliefs either. Several "facts" in the original version of this article have subsequently needed revision, which is exactly how good science is supposed to work. Nothing lasts forever, including some of the most well-known findings in the history of psychology research!
