item.title: The Perfect Pillow Trap: Finding Unexpected Wisdom in Discomfort
item.description:
Wisdom

The Perfect Pillow Trap: Finding Unexpected Wisdom in Discomfort

Sometimes, in trying to find relief, we intensify and prolong our discomfort.

Posted November 12, 2026

Key points
  • Shifting your relationship with discomfort can create room for learning, growth, and transformation.
  • Some types of discomfort can facilitate the attainment of a more enlightened way of being in the world.
  • Ironically, many of our efforts to avoid discomfort merely serve to intensify our suffering.
Source: Gromobo / Pixabay

What if shifting your relationship with discomfort could simultaneously ease its intensity and create room for learning, growth, and transformation?

The Urge to Escape Discomfort

Our culture values convenience, comfort, speed, short-term gains, accumulation, and immediate relief.

When physical or psychological discomfort arises, we instinctively try to eliminate it via:

  • Resisting or distracting ourselves
  • Analyzing or seeking control
  • Searching for the perfect solution or acting prematurely

Not All Discomfort Is the Same

I’m not suggesting that we welcome all discomfort or simply learn to live with it. It’s important to recognize the difference among:

  • Physical discomfort and pain that signals an injury or illness
  • Psychological pain from a toxic relationship or circumstance that needs to change
  • Discomfort that opens the way to learning, growth, and transformation

What I am suggesting is that sometimes, in trying so hard to find relief, we unintentionally intensify our discomfort and prolong its effects.

Setting

My relationship with physical and psychological discomfort was profoundly transformed during my initial 10-day silent meditation retreat. Participants entered the retreat center with a commitment to stay for the entire 10 days. We were required to relinquish our technology, assigned a cell-like sleeping space, and provided with a brief retreat overview.

Imagine a peaceful minimalist meditation hall, assigned meditation mats for each participant, and an outside shed filled with extra mats, pillows, and blankets. Fourteen hours of daily meditation with brief breaks. Two vegetarian meals per day. No technology, talking, reading, exercising, or familiar distractions allowed. In short, your basic meditation bootcamp.

Discomfort

As the days passed, my physical and psychological discomfort grew. The “silent” retreat hall included a soundtrack comprised of frequent outbursts of belching, passing gas, desperate shifting bodies, and deep sighs and moans.

Despite decades of meditation practice, I soon felt the physical and psychological strain and pain of sitting cross-legged for hours. My body was shouting “enough,” while my mind intensely revisited past challenges, failures, and unfinished business.

Quest

I had no idea how to manage the pain. During each brief break, I rummaged in the shed for the perfect combination of pillows to ease my rapidly expanding physical discomfort and psychological distress. I was determined and optimistically certain that the ideal pillow combination existed and that I would find it.

By day four, 20 pillows of various shapes and sizes crowded my meditation mat. Increasingly desperate for comfort, I fervently continued my pillow arrangement mission, unsuccessfully creating and assessing one combination after another.

Critical Mass

None of the pillow combinations worked. My physical discomfort and psychological stress kept growing. Although I remained committed to staying for the entire retreat, I had no idea how I would make it through. And then something miraculously shifted.

Shift

On day five, my pillow quest unexpectedly gave way to releasing. My body and psyche elegantly eased into the meditation sessions. The quality of my discomfort and my relationship to it changed. During the breaks, I found myself returning my stash of pillows, one by one, to the shed.

Rather than finding the perfect pillow combination, I discovered something more powerful: Discomfort and comfort are always in flow. As my relationship with discomfort changed, my experience of it shifted, and my suffering was diminished.

Resistance

Our instinct and attempts to mitigate or eliminate discomfort often serve to intensify it. We tense and adjust, ruminate, distract, seek immediate relief, make premature decisions, and attempt to control. Our vigorous efforts merely serve to intensify our suffering.

Allowing

Allowing means acknowledging our experience without immediately judging it or trying to fix, change, or escape it. It does not mean resigning ourselves to our experience or even liking it.

Through the practice of active inquiry, we can observe our discomfort with curiosity:

  • What am I noticing in my experience right now?
  • How does my experience change when I stop fighting it?
  • What might this discomfort be telling me?

Releasing

Releasing cannot be forced. It unfolds as we loosen our attachment to a specific goal, outcome, expectation, timing, or meaning. As I naturally let go of my quest for the perfect pillow combination and sat with my discomfort, its intensity eased.

Understanding

Discomfort does not automatically provide a direct path to wisdom. It can, however, provide the opportunity for understanding and transformation. Through releasing resistance to discomfort, room is created to pause, listen, and allow something better suited to emerge in our various life realms.

Transformation

Growth and transformation become possible when we approach discomfort with curiosity, awareness, openness, cognitive flexibility, and a commitment to learning. Consider what various forms of discomfort invite us to explore:

  • Physical: listening to our body’s needs and limits.
  • Relational: patterns, boundary violations, and misalignments.
  • Emotional: fear, grief, unmet needs, and outdated beliefs and values.
  • Professional: obsolete identities, value conflicts, misalignment, and the need for change.

Perfect Pillow Lessons

At the beginning of the retreat, I naively thought the perfect combination of pillows would empower me to eradicate my discomfort. I searched, collected, experimented, and assessed. The harder I tried to control discomfort, the more powerless I felt. As I began to release control and sit with my experience, the intensity, quality, and meaning of my discomfort began to shift and transform.

How often do we try to manage life’s discomforts by accumulating “pillows”—material goods, distractions, quick fixes, expectations, control attempts?

Invitation to Reflect

I’m a fan of comfort, not an advocate for doing without it. My invitation is simply to notice when seeking comfort serves us and when it gets in the way of learning, growth, and transformation.

Trying to avoid discomfort at all costs can be physically and emotionally exhausting. Approaching it with curiosity, awareness, openness, flexibility, and a sense of humor about our shared humanity can create the requisite time and space for transformation.

I invite you to pause and ask yourself:

  • Where am I using too much energy to avoid, eliminate, or control discomfort?
  • What “pillows” have I collected or attempted to collect to find relief?
  • What might be possible for me if I stopped searching for the next perfect pillow?

item.title: What Perpetuates the Family Cycle of Violence?
item.description:
Family Dynamics

What Perpetuates the Family Cycle of Violence?

Using computer models to unpack critical factors in the family cycle of violence.

Posted November 12, 2026

Key points
  • The family cycle of violence is difficult to study across multiple generations.
  • Most parents with maltreatment histories do not become child abusers.
  • Agent-based models allow researchers to investigate pathways perpetuating the family cycle of violence.

This post is the second in an occasional series on the family cycle of violence.

In May 2026, we posted "Do Abused Parents Become Child Abusers?" which we subtitled: "Multiple interacting factors shape the intergenerational cycle of maltreatment." That post is intended to be the foundation for an undetermined number of future posts examining the intergenerational transmission of increased risk for maltreatment to the offspring of parents who were maltreated themselves as children. The larger focus of this series is the two-part question: “Can we break the family cycle of violence?” and “If so, how?”

The key points of the earlier post are that the single most powerful risk factor for a child being maltreated is having a parent who was maltreated. Most (~70 percent) parents with child maltreatment histories do not become abusive parents. However, the risk of becoming an abusive parent is 6 to 12 times higher than for parents without a childhood maltreatment history. The mechanisms underlying this increased risk may be indirect (e.g., decreased parental vigilance) or direct (perpetration). This increased risk is a result of multiple, interacting levels of factors (e.g., depression, dissociation, substance abuse, domestic violence, unsafe households, poverty, neighborhood factors, public policies). To be cost-effective, prevention programs must seek to address the most critical shared underlying factors synergistically.

The post also notes that individuals can promote positive social change by openly acknowledging their own and others’ childhood maltreatment, thereby validating survivors, reducing stigma, and keeping public attention focused on this enormous public health problem.

The Critical Factors That Perpetuate Intergenerational Transmission of Risk

How do we tease out the most critical factors on which to focus the always limited prevention resources? This conundrum is further complicated by the need to follow these multiple interacting factors in large general population samples for decades. Not to mention that even the most dedicated family violence researchers are lifetime-limited to studying only two or three generations during their careers.

This seems like an impossible task!

Another Way

There is another way, however, to get at least a ballpark understanding of the interacting factors that promote the family cycle of violence across generations. This involves the use of Agent-Based Models. ABMs are computer simulations in which individual “people” are represented by computational entities (agents) that can behave and interact with each other according to predefined rules (Smaldino, 2023). Think SimCity or other computer games that involve characters with past histories, have current and future agendas, and develop complicated interrelationships that can evolve apart and together “over time” to produce a range of outcomes.

Computer simulations, both equation-based and agent-based, are widely used to investigate systems and processes that are too large, too complex, and too costly to study on real-world scales. Examples include the weather, epidemics, and the Big Bang. One advantage is that computer simulations can be run thousands of times as needed to sweep through the numerous combinations of potential variables, searching for fundamental trajectories, collapses, singularities, best fits with real-world data, and critical tipping points that may serve as prevention targets.

Agent-Based Simulations of the Family Cycle of Violence

Perhaps the best way to understand an ABM is to briefly describe a model simulating the intergenerational transmission of risk for maltreatment of offspring. The model begins with a number of unmarried adult males and females (typically 50 each to limit CPU time, as this breeds hundreds of new agents over three to five generations). These male and female adults are randomly scattered on a multicolored checkerboard “city” map of neighborhoods that hold different levels of risk for children born in them.

In generation 0, each agent (males are blue, females green) is randomly assigned a lifespan and a level of positive and negative “childhood” baggage, some of which may be passed to offspring. These adults proceed to seek out an opposite-gender partner with which to have “children.” Each adult can “see” the childhood baggage of the adults immediately around them and chooses a partner based on a variable called “match” (more on “match” below).

If there is not a suitable “match” in sight, agents take off randomly seeking one. Some agents never meet their “match” and never have children. In addition, each agent is randomly assigned a lifespan at birth. When their lifespan is up, they die and are removed from the board.

When a pair of agents do match—that is, their combined childhood baggage is within the bounds set by the “match” variable—they can “marry,” and every so often they breed a child. They also move around as a family, landing in positive or negative neighborhoods, which affect their growing children. The children pass through three developmental stages (infancy, childhood, adolescence), eventually becoming adults who carry forward into the next generation the risk accumulated over their childhoods. Childhood risk may be concentrated at certain developmental stages or distributed randomly across development, with the weight that earlier acquired risk has a greater lifetime impact.

When the adolescents become young adults, they leave their families to seek a partner with which to have their own children. A new “generation” occurs when a specified percentage (typically 70 percent) of children born to the preceding generation have reached adulthood. Models are typically run for three to five generations, and a combination of inputs is examined for their effects on outputs such as percent of population abused, average risk scores, female-to-male victim ratios, or geographic density of abuse/non-abuse clusters.

A typical experiment involves sweeping through a pre-set combination of variables (e.g., threshold for domestic violence, gender sensitivity coefficients, degree of match) to see how various combinations affect selected outputs. Typically, each combination of inputs is run at least 100 times, and the results are saved to a file for detailed statistical analyses.

Assortative Mating

The “match” variable was included among the input parameters because of research on the nonrandom or “assortative” mating of individuals with mental health diagnoses. Epidemiologists have found that individuals with mental health diagnoses are significantly more likely to partner with mates who have the same or related diagnoses than are comparison subjects with medical diagnoses having similar degrees of lifestyle impact, such as diabetes or epilepsy. Large-scale Swedish studies have found the frequency of assortative mating for 11 major mental health conditions ranges between two and six times that of equivalent medical conditions (Nordsletten et al., 2016).

“All computer models are wrong, but some are useful” —Old programmer saying

Somewhat to my surprise, “match” has turned out to be a critical variable driving rates of intergenerational transmission of risk for maltreatment of offspring. The ABM finds that the impact of two parents with childhood maltreatment histories significantly increases the risk that their offspring will also suffer maltreatment. Much of this effect is driven by the increased rate of domestic violence found when both parents have a childhood maltreatment history.

Thus, among the potential insights gained from the ABM model is that a childhood history of maltreatment in both parents is potentially a major risk factor for continuation of the family cycle of violence. How often this double parental maltreatment history occurs in real life is difficult to establish at present. However, if we accept that the assortative mating research on psychiatric diagnoses also applies to some degree to individuals with trauma-associated psychiatric disorders, it could happen among a significant number of family violence cases.

Computer models are “thinking machines.” They require their authors to think through dynamic processes and to formulate and parameterize the resulting algorithms. An ABM model is not real life, but sometimes it can yield insights that would be impossible to glean from real life without investing many years and millions of dollars.

item.title: The Universality of Privilege and Inheritance of Excellence
item.description:
Creativity

The Universality of Privilege and Inheritance of Excellence

Accomplishment and privilege are among the oldest features of civilization.

Posted November 12, 2026

Key points
  • Countless innovations delivered immense benefits and privileges.
  • The printing press accelerated the growth and transmission of knowledge.
  • The greatest privilege is that each generation inherits the achievements of those who came before it.
Source: Gerd Altmann / Pixabay

The word privilege has somehow evolved linguistically to be viewed negatively. It has also come to imply an unearned advantage or an unfair benefit held by one group at another's expense.

Throughout human history, privilege has meant something quite different: privilege has emerged when individuals and/or groups apply merit, achievement, competence, and excellence in ways that expand possibilities for everyone. I refer to this as the MACE Principle.

Research shows that high levels of expertize and exceptional performance emerge through sustained practice, learning, and skill refinement rather than arising spontaneously. In this sense, such accomplishments and the benefits they create for subsequent generations are among the oldest features of human civilization (Ericsson, 2008; Srivastava & Das, 2015).

The Collective Gained a Privilege

Nearly three million years ago, our distant ancestors fashioned the first stone tools. The first person to shape stone into a cutting implement created something far more significant than a simple object. That innovation gave the entire group a practical advantage.

The collective also gained a privilege. The tribe could now cut hunted and gathered food and, self-evidently, share their food far more efficiently and much more quickly. Survival itself became easier.

Consequently, the privilege created by that stone-tool innovation was not confined to the inventor; it became a significant benefit and privilege enjoyed by the collective (Kivell, 2015; Stout, 2011).

The same pattern recurs throughout history. The invention of the wheel transformed transport and trade. Once developed, the wheel's benefits and the privilege it created extended far beyond its creator.

Entire communities far removed from the original invention gained the privilege of moving goods and people more efficiently. What began as an achievement of human ingenuity became a shared privilege and an immense social advantage beyond its original location (Kivell, 2015; Stout, 2011).

The Printing Press

Perhaps no invention demonstrates this process more dramatically than the printing press. Developed in the 15th century by Johannes Gutenberg in Mainz, within the Holy Roman Empire (present-day Germany), the printing press fundamentally altered humanity's relationship with the development and advancement of knowledge.

Reading, writing, collective information, ideas, and knowledge, once largely confined to a comparatively small number of individuals, could now be reproduced, preserved, and distributed on a scale that was never before possible.

Reading and writing ceased to be “a mystery” for a select number of individuals or a “select” group. As with the stone tool and the wheel before it, the printing press created new benefits and privileges, consequently moving these benefits and privileges from the few to the many.

Although history informs us (as with all inventions and achievements), the resulting benefits and privileges were not always distributed equally.

However, even with this being the case, with the wider dissemination of knowledge (following the invention of the 15th-century printing press), the benefits of this invention extended far beyond Gutenberg and transformed what future generations could achieve (Jara-Figueroa et al., 2019; Triggle & Triggle, 2017).

Time

Consider what followed. For approximately three million years, humanity crafted tools, built settlements, established civilizations, constructed cities, developed metallurgy, crossed oceans, fought wars, and created empires.

During this period, countless innovations delivered immense benefits and privilege. Yet the accumulation and transmission of knowledge remained comparatively limited.

Then, within about five centuries of the invention of the printing press, humanity witnessed an unprecedented acceleration in the growth and development of knowledge (Jara-Figueroa et al., 2019; Triggle & Triggle, 2017).

In the 18th century, Edward Jenner laid the foundations of modern immunization with the first successful smallpox vaccination (Riedel, 2005).

In the 20th century, the United States sent three men to the Moon: Neil Armstrong, the first human to walk on its surface; Buzz Aldrin, the second; and Michael Collins, who remained in lunar orbit as part of the mission.

These achievements produced further benefits and privilege, as earlier innovations had. They reflected humanity's expanding capacity to preserve, transmit, and build upon knowledge. The printing press transformed reading, writing, ideas, and information into a far more widely shared social benefit and privilege for the many (Triggle & Triggle, 2017).

In doing so, it expanded the benefits and privilege available to successive generations and helped create the conditions for scientific, technological, and civilizational advancement to proceed at a pace previously unknown in human history (Jara-Figueroa et al., 2019; Triggle & Triggle, 2017).

The same principle applied across medicine, engineering, agriculture, chemistry, and countless other fields.

Vaccines, clean water systems, supermarkets, automobiles, telecommunications, digital technologies, and now artificial intelligence all exist because individuals pursued excellence in their respective domains.

The benefits of those achievements are enjoyed not merely by their creators but by millions, and even potentially billions, of people (Tewksbury et al., 1980; Yu & Liu, 2021).

Throughout history, parents have generally sought to provide advantages, opportunities, benefits, and privilege to their children, just as previous generations sought to provide them to those who followed.

Civilization itself can therefore be understood as the cumulative result of countless individuals attempting to improve the circumstances inherited by the next generation (Gulyas & Powell, 2019; Stout & Hecht, 2017).

This does not self-evidently mean that every benefit or privilege is distributed equally; it never has and it never will.

Change

It does mean, however, that inventions and achievements, no matter what they were, enriched lives, from the smallest tribes to the largest civilizations, because there were individuals who invented something that changed what previously existed, and with this, benefits and privilege arose (Dean et al., 2014; Tewksbury et al., 1980).

The story of human civilization is the story of expanding everyone's potential for privilege, but not a guarantee. Through innovation, discovery, and excellence, however, humanity has repeatedly turned extraordinary achievements into benefits that potentially eventually become available to the broader populace.

The greatest privilege is that each generation inherits the achievements of those who came before and can contribute new ones for those yet to come (Dean et al., 2014; Stout & Hecht, 2017).

item.title: I Am Turning 40, and Refusing to Apologize for It
item.description:
Personal Perspectives

I Am Turning 40, and Refusing to Apologize for It

Personal Perspective: Reflections on turning 40 and all I have overcome.

Posted November 12, 2026

Key points
  • We are constantly told to fear and dread aging.
  • As I turn 40 this month, I reflect on all I have overcome to get here. And how much I have grown.
  • Celebrating ourselves can be a way of honoring our own journeys.
Reflecting during my birthday month
Source: Kaytee Gillis

November is my birthday month.

Yes, I celebrate the month. (Don’t @ me!) It was actually something I started doing in college. My birthday (the actual day) falls close to Thanksgiving, so many of my friends would be leaving campus right around the time I was getting ready to celebrate. I also had a roommate whose birthday was close to Christmas, so we started celebrating early.

The trend caught on (whether it caught on or I pushed it, I will never know). This worked well until my 21st birthday, which, as we all know, cannot legally be celebrated early—at least not if you want your special bar drink in hand.

If you’re rolling your eyes and thinking I appear a bit arrogant, bear with me for a moment while I explain. While celebrating and having fun with friends was, of course, fun, these celebrations actually served a deeper purpose for me—although I didn't know it at the time. When college ended, I found myself alone again, thrown back into a world where my only source of support—my family—was unsafe and unstable. Home was scary.

Celebrating myself became a way of honoring my own journey. It was a way of recognizing the strength it took to navigate the year, and the safety I was learning to create within myself. It became a "Yay, Kaytee, you made it another year. You did it." Years later, I still have that same message, but it has become something deeper.

This was almost 20 years ago. This month I turn 40. An age where we, especially women, are told to stop celebrating. An age we are taught to dread. All month, I’ve received messages like these from others, including my own family:

“I bet you’re not excited about this birthday.”

"I was going to send you a card, but I imagine you don't want the reminder."

“I bet you won’t celebrate the whole month anymore.”

“We can just pretend you’re 39 again!”

And I can’t help but wonder: Why? Why are we so negative about aging? We mourn when people die young, yet somehow shame those of us who are fortunate enough to keep living. We grieve the years someone never got to experience, while simultaneously treating the years we do get as something to fear.

I refuse to participate in this ageism. I have always celebrated my birthday, and I always will. Not just in the traditional, celebratory sense (I mean, cake is always nice), but as a way of honoring myself and all that I have become. I am always stumped at how much it bothers people that I dare embrace myself as an aging woman.

I am proud of who I am today. I love myself more today than I ever did when I was young. I no longer self-medicate or mistreat my body in the ways I had to to survive my childhood. I am happier and healthier now than I ever have been before. I have come so far and learned so much since that 20-year-old college student who celebrated her birthday with her roommates for a week straight, in one of the few places where she felt safe (but was unable to verbalize this at the time). I wish I could go back and tell her that someday it won't be so scary, and she won't have to put on a fake persona of strength to continue the denial. I would tell her not only that she would survive, but how much she would survive, and how much of a life she would eventually build for herself. I think she would be pretty damn proud, too. (And maybe a bit relieved to see a light at the end of what felt like a long, dark tunnel.)

Happy birthday month to me. And to all of us who have survived and are surviving. I hope you find a way to honor and celebrate yourself, too.

item.title: 3 Anxiety Resets From an OCD Therapist With OCD
item.description:
OCD

3 Anxiety Resets From an OCD Therapist With OCD

Even therapists get anxious. Here are my go-to techniques.

Posted November 12, 2026

Key points
  • Butterfly tapping is a subtle, easy-to-use self-soothing technique when your nervous system is activated.
  • Supportive thought mantras can help you redirect automatic, negative thinking patterns.
  • The container exercise is a practical and useful visualization tool from EMDR therapy.
Knife exposures are a common type of intervention for harm OCD.
Source: Mart Production / Pexels

“Sorry, my hand is shaking,” my client says.

We are in the middle of an exposure exercise for his obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). He experiences terrifying intrusive thoughts about harming his loved ones, and my job is to help him confront those fears without resorting to compulsions. My client is holding a knife to the small of my back.

“I know it's hard, but stay with the exposure for another minute,” I reply.

As I sit with my client and allow the anxiety of the moment to wash over him, I ask my client to rate his distress on a scale of 1 to 10.

I am an OCD therapist, and I practice an objectively strange type of therapy. I help my clients engage in exposures—brave acts that fly in the face of their fears—while resisting their compulsions.

I love being an OCD therapist. Exposure and response prevention (ERP) is vastly preferable to trying to talk my clients out of their fears. Reassurance rarely works for long. The only thing that can convince my client that he won’t hurt me is being in a position where he could.

My clients are kindhearted, earnest humans who suffer from the same disorder that made me feel alone and scared for most of my 20s. The fear of harming someone does not equate to the intent to harm someone. I myself grappled mightily with this confusing thought pattern and learned to trust myself again.

But there are moments when my professionalism and empathy come up against a formidable foe: my own nervous system.

Sometimes, my nervous system forgets that I am safe. Sometimes my nervous system doesn’t understand time and place and, most importantly for the knife exposure, context. Despite all the work I've done, I still experience fear, anxiety, doubt, and the occasional panic attack.

And my experience is not unique. Many therapists are wounded healers. We love this work because we have lived this work.

One thing I've learned about mental health recovery is that we are never done. The goal isn't to eliminate anxiety forever. It's to develop the tools to move through it without allowing it to control our lives.

When I cannot stay present and grounded for my own therapy session, I count on three resourcing techniques that I learned from eye movement desensitization and reprocessing (EMDR), a therapy technique that I underwent as a patient. When my body forgets my professional training, I use techniques from EMDR to guide myself back to the present moment.

Here are some of my favorites:

Cross your arms and alternate tapping on either side of the body.
Source: Darina Belonogova / Pexels

1. Subtle Butterfly Tapping

Butterfly tapping is a technique that involves gently alternating taps on either side of the body. It's a subtle movement you can try almost anywhere, including at a crowded party or during a stressful conversation. (Or, in my case, in a knife exposure with my client)

Cross your arms against your chest and place each hand on the opposite collarbone. Now, gently and rhythmically begin alternating taps from one side to the other.

Continue for a short period, noticing the rhythm and how your body responds.

The alternating stimulation and repetitive movement may help you feel more grounded. There is no need to force yourself to feel calm or continue if the exercise feels uncomfortable.

Sometimes, a moment of physical connection is all you need to find your footing again.

2. Supportive Thought Mantra

Your mind can be remarkably unkind, especially when you feel anxious. Trauma can encode negative thought patterns into your brain, telling you things like “I cannot handle feeling uncomfortable” or “I am not strong enough.”

Before heading into a stressful situation, you can choose a phrase that reminds you of how you want to respond when discomfort arises.

Try something like:

  • “I can feel anxious and still be present.”
  • “I can be scared and safe.”
  • “I can handle bad feelings.”

Repeat your phrase gently when you need a reminder.

I like to take a photo of my mantra and set it as my phone's home screen because I tend to pick up my phone and glance at it when I'm uncomfortable.

An important distinction for anyone with OCD: A mantra should offer encouragement, not become a ritual you must repeat until your fear disappears. The aim is to develop tolerance for uncomfortable feelings, not compulsively reassure ourselves that nothing bad will happen.

For this exercise, visualize any container that can easily come to mind.
Source: William Finn / Pexels

3. Container Visualization

EMDR can open up strong emotions, but it also guides people on how to temporarily put them away.

For this exercise, you may close your eyes, if appropriate in the situation, and imagine a container that can hold the feelings or concerns you aren't ready to address.

It can be a chest, lockbox, jar, drawer, or anything you can vividly picture.

Now imagine placing a troubling experience inside that container. You can return to the experience later, when you have the time and resources for processing.

I use this for a nervous system spike during my therapy workday. My job is to stay present for my client, so I put any reactions in a container and set them aside temporarily.

The goal isn't to suppress feelings or avoid necessary emotional work. If you have OCD, be mindful that this exercise doesn't become another way to neutralize intrusive thoughts or escape uncertainty.

Instead, think of it as giving yourself permission to choose when and how to address an experience that deserves your attention.

Staying With the Discomfort

As an OCD therapist, I have learned that recovery doesn't mean becoming a person who never experiences anxiety.

In fact, the entire premise of ERP is that we can learn to face discomfort without relying on compulsions to make it disappear.

The three techniques can offer support when anxiety feels overwhelming, but they aren't substitutes for treatment. No anxiety reset should become a ritual that you perform perfectly.

By the end of our session, my client's hand is no longer shaking. He tells me his distress has fallen to a “2 out of 10.”

“Good job staying with the discomfort,” I say, mostly to him, but also a bit to myself.

Here we are, two imperfect nervous systems, finding our way back to the present moment and moving forward with recovery.

item.title: The Ultimate Wounded Healer: Remembering Marsha Linehan
item.description:
Wisdom

The Ultimate Wounded Healer: Remembering Marsha Linehan

Marsha Linehan turned her own pain into a lifeline for millions.

Posted November 12, 2026

Key points
  • Carl Jung introduced the term “wounded healer” to capture the essence of the archetype embodied by Chiron.
  • Jung believed that “disease of the soul” might be the most valuable training for a healer.
  • A living embodiment of Chiron, Marsha Linehan spent 30 years giving suicidal patients a reason to live.

The mental health community is mourning the loss of Marsha Linehan, the pioneering American psychologist who created dialectical behavior therapy (DBT). Having openly lived with borderline personality disorder—often understood in clinical circles as profound, complex trauma—she embodied the true archetype of the wounded healer. Drawing directly from the depths of her own darkest struggles, she forged a compassionate, life-saving clinical framework that transformed modern psychotherapy and empowered countless individuals to build lives worth living.

Carl Jung’s Wounded Healer Archetype: Wisdom Through Suffering

Carl Jung first introduced the term “wounded healer” to capture the essence of the archetype embodied by Chiron in Greek Mythology. Jung believed that “disease of the soul” might be the most valuable training for a healer because pain often brings with it profound wisdom and understanding. Through navigating their personal experiences of suffering and adversity, the wounded healer can acquire a profound understanding that suffering, compassion, and the journey toward resilience can only be accessed by living through pain. Within the darkest moments of suffering and despair, unexpected clarity and hidden truths can come to light.

As counterintuitive as it may sound, from tragedy and trauma can come a sacred invitation to grow, evolve, and build wisdom. When hope seems dim, the difficulties you encounter may lead you to a moment of self- examination, an opportunity to look within that may cause you to pause and unravel the lessons hidden within your life’s experiences. Your wounds, rather than simply serving as reminders of past suffering, can transform into wisdom, serving as a compass that directs you toward crafting a life rich in meaning, true fulfillment, and joy. Pain enhances our capacity to empathize and relate to others.

Finding Resilience and Purpose Through Healing Others

In Greek Myth of Chiron, we find that enduring hardship can serve as a sacred key to personal evolution; it teaches us that amid our deepest emotional suffering lies the golden opportunity to awaken profound resilience and compassion and, most importantly, to illuminate the path to understanding our true purpose in life. A living embodiment of Chiron, Linehan spent 30 years giving severely suicidal patients a reason to live.

Every human experience, from the cradle to the grave, includes some form of suffering or painful and unpredictable life circumstances. Pain is an unavoidable and universal part of being human and requires acknowledgment and understanding instead of being ignored or pushed aside. In the midst of his pain, Chiron found meaning in his ability to heal others, transforming his own suffering into a source of strength that allowed him to connect deeply with those around him. Chiron’s story teaches us that even in the depths of despair, we can find purpose through our suffering. His journey illustrates that personal growth often arises from embracing our pain, learning to heal, and using our experiences to guide and uplift others. This emphasizes the importance of resilience, compassion, and the transformative power of self-acceptance in leading a meaningful life.

Through his tale, we learn that even amid the heaviest darkness, the light of hope can pierce through and offer a pathway to personal growth. Often, the most compassionate and impactful healers are those who have faced their own struggles, as their personal wounds enable them to connect deeply with others who are suffering. May this remind you that even in your own personal suffering, there is potential for growth.

Through my work, I have witnessed the undeniable power that humans have to adapt to, navigate, and even grow from life’s most painful events. When I sit across from a person as they slowly navigate their pain and suffering, I serve as the compassionate witness and guide, eagerly observing the gradual but profound growth that can occur. I believe that the most beautiful thing in the world is seeing the light come into someone’s eyes after they have been lost in the darkness of despair for so long. Witnessing this process feels magical.

Trauma, tragedy, and deep grief all have a way of pushing a person way beyond their comfort zone. It urges you to confront fears and insecurities, but ultimately the journey through pain becomes a sacred teacher, one that illuminates the path to greater self-discovery and awakening. When questioned about his renowned David, the celebrated Renaissance sculptor and poet Michelangelo famously remarked, “I saw the angel in the marble and carved until I set him free.” This insightful quote captures Michelangelo’s conviction that the sculpture lies within the marble block, awaiting revelation through the artist’s craftsmanship. Like Michelangelo, I have focused my life’s work on chiseling away at the unresolved trauma of my clients, cautiously dismantling their defense mechanisms and fears, and gently peeling back the layers of shame to unveil the “authentic self” buried beneath, patiently waiting to be rediscovered and embraced. Within the human psyche exists an innate healing wisdom. As you navigate fears and insecurities, you may uncover a strength you never knew you possessed, a newfound clarity that helps you to transform your pain into purpose, or even a deeper insight that reshapes your struggle into a source of deep meaning. Pain serves as a powerful initiation in the soul’s journey, acting as a catalyst for transformation and growth.

item.title: Moving by Numbers: The Trap of the Easily Measurable
item.description:
Conscientiousness

Moving by Numbers: The Trap of the Easily Measurable

Activity tracking may be a reward with a built-in expiry date

Posted November 12, 2026

Key points
  • Changes caused by diet/exercise self-monitoring decline after tracking stops.
  • Mere measurability may be biasing research and individuals towards monotonous forms of behaviour change.
  • Focusing on measurability may sideline more sustainable reasons for change, whether intrinsic or extrinsic.

This post is part of a series. Read part one here.

In the previous post in this series on eating and moving by numbers, we reviewed many years of research (including hundreds of individual studies and over a dozen meta-analyses) on how tracking and quantification affect diet and exercise. And we found that the answer is, on average and in aggregate, “not much”.

In this post, I’ll explore a simple two-pronged hypothesis that’s compatible with that research literature, though not proven by it: that measuring allows you to change 1) only what is easily measurable and 2) only for as long as you keep measuring it.

This idea is sparked by the observation from last time that although none of the results from these meta-analyses of self-monitoring studies are particularly substantial, the biggest, clearest effect is that steps taken seem to increase while step-counting is happening. This raises the possibility that the tracking has more of an effect here because the behaviour of walking is more directly, simply, and meaningfully countable than other kinds of movement are, and a lot more so than eating is. A relatively simple machine can distinguish a step from a non-step, and once it has, then no more human effort is required: you walk, the machine records.

All other kinds of movement are trickier to track than a pace. For example, a recent New York Times article on “Why Weight Lifting Is Good for Your Heart” noted that the constraints and biases of measurement technology are one reason for the persistent sidelining of strength training in research on cardiovascular benefits of exercise: “One of the limitations of studying resistance training—and why it’s taken scientists so long to understand its benefit for the heart—is that exercises like squats and bench presses are hard to track with a wearable device. That means scientists must rely on self-reported data.” It’s frustrating to think just how much mere measurability has helped skew decades’ worth of public health advice towards endurance cardio and away from forms of movement that are increasingly recognised to offer a wider range of benefits.

The difficulty of measuring is even greater with eating than with squatting or cycling or skiing. Because you’re measuring the nutrition ingested rather than the behaviour of ingesting it, a lot more hassle is involved: measuring and weighing amounts of ingredients, calculating energy provision and macronutrient balance, comparing the amount of food prepared versus consumed. The sheer complication of committing to meaningful tracking of one’s eating is one reason why I think its cost/benefit ratio tends to be so poor, in ways I’ll explore in the next part in this series.

So the first step of our inference is that when you use measurement to incentivize change, the changes you end up incentivizing most are not the ones you care most about, the ones that will have the most benefits for anything else in your life—they’re merely the ones you can most easily measure. This leads to a second hypothesis, less directly supported by the existing evidence but certainly not contradicted by it: that these maximally measurable changes may be the least likely to be preserved after the measuring stops.

The formal follow-up data are patchy in general, and they seem to show significant decline across all the habits and “benefits” being studied; after you take away the measurement framework, things seem to revert to baseline at some point between quite slowly and very quickly!

(For example, Vetrovksy et al. (2022), analysing 75 studies, of which 24 included a follow-up phase, found that the step-count increase more than halved in a median of 12 weeks’ follow-up. Chaudhry et al. (2020), analysing 57 studies, report that within two years the increase is down to 10% of the four-month level, and by three to four years people are back to where they started. Freak-Poli et al. (2020), analysing 14 studies, report no change even at short follow-up points.)

Especially given that no other behaviours showed much change to begin with, we can’t confidently conclude anything about how the increases in step count decay relative to changes in other activities. Still, we might speculate that being guided by mere measurability entails a downplaying of other reasons why people might keep doing things: intrinsic rewards like in-the-moment pleasure, good fit with lifestyle and interests and environment, and good fit also with specific health and fitness goals.

Nothing against walking; I just published a personal blog post on what a lovely context it can be for thinking, and it can be delightful in many other ways too. But those delights are, I suspect, mostly not encouraged by the “how many steps have I taken?” lens. When done for counting’s sake, walking may foreground primarily the very quality of monotony that makes it so easy to measure.

A knowledgeable reader (Emily Nicholas Angl) shared an interesting extension of this thought: that immediate “improvements” generated by tracking technologies may have the exact opposite effects over the long term. It’s possible that where counting is strongly emphasised, there’s almost inevitably poor intrinsic drive to maintain the new habit, because the counting has been over-relied on to do all the incentivizing work—and has been applied only to activities that are uncomplicated enough to be readily measured. In this sense, the initial rewards may themselves become the vulnerability.

Looking at this research, it’s instructive to turn our attention to what’s being overshadowed by the quantification. In one paper I included in the review last time (Ferguson et al., 2022), there was a suggestion that quality of life tends to get ignored in the research because it takes longest to change. My intuition as a coach would be the opposite: that if you make changes that are genuinely right for you, greater happiness (or contentment, or purposefulness, etc) is likely to be an almost immediate result—indeed, that intending to enhance everyday experience should be a guide to which changes to make in the first place, because they’re the ones that are likeliest to get embedded and stay there. From this perspective, increasing day-to-day satisfaction is not a nice-to-have that may trickle in eventually, far “downstream” of the solid behavioural changes that really count. Instead, the very experience of having started doing it becomes the reason to keep doing it.

The absence of any mention of participants’ experiences of the changes being measured therefore seems telling in itself: it supports the idea of an overreliance on one ultra-simplistic extrinsic reward (the number) at the expense of any intrinsic rewards, and, in many cases, also of more personally meaningful extrinsic rewards (like specific kinds of ability regained or possibility unlocked). One might extrapolate from here to the benefits that mixed-methods research (including both quantitative measures and qualitative inquiry into participant experiences) could offer to medical research if it turned from an outlier to the norm.

A final dimension I’d like to weave into these speculations about why people do and don’t do the thing we’re asking them to and getting them to measure themselves doing is the question of individual attitude differences. I found myself wondering, as I trawled through the meta-analyses, whether what’s really being assessed in this research is less the cleverness of the tech in getting lazy, greedy humans to be more active and abstemious, but the pre-existing inclination of said humans to be more or less conscientious about the thing they’ve signed up for.

The differences between “compliers” and “non-compliers” (including “defiers”) are well documented as a confounding factor in health research. But I didn’t see any explicit acknowledgement of these dynamics in this literature, despite some studies finding big differences between “high-adherence” and “low-adherence” individuals (the most striking I found being Bertoli et al., 2025, where the former lost an average of 7 kg and the latter 3.5 kg over six months). As a participant, you get out what you put in—but you may not continue to once the study structures are over. And by definition, conscientious compliers won’t keep complying when there’s nothing to comply with! So if all that were driving the changes was conscientious compliance to a tenuous numerical rule, then once the study ends and the rule is lifted, the reasons to continue may seem similarly flimsy.

item.title: I Used to Drink to Fit In. Here’s What I Wish I Knew
item.description:
Alcoholism

I Used to Drink to Fit In. Here’s What I Wish I Knew

Drinking to fit in can keep us from finding true belonging

Posted November 12, 2026

“I am afraid if I stop drinking, I won’t be able to fit in anymore” is a common fear many of my clients have when they are considering cutting alcohol out of their lives.

If you have ever felt this way, you are not alone. I know that fear well. For a long time, I believed that I needed to fit in to belong, and I’d do anything I could to meet other people's expectations, whether that meant putting on a bubbly mask, faking interest in topics I had no passion for, or having a drink in my hand when I was trying to drink less.

When we live in a culture where drinking is part of everyday life, choosing to opt out of alcohol is not just a practical decision, but also a social one. It can feel almost like a threat to our sense of belonging and social standing.

The Belief: I Have to Drink to Fit In

It makes sense. Many of us have learned that drinking helps us fit in. Maybe you learned that sipping a club soda at a party where everyone is drinking beer makes you feel like an outsider. Perhaps you've discovered that a couple of drinks can make you more bubbly or extraverted. Or you have found that a glass of wine is the trick to faking enthusiasm for a topic you have no interest in.

Drinking is not only a way to participate in the cultural norm, but it can also feel like a shortcut to help us bring out the version of ourselves that is deemed more “socially desirable” by mainstream culture and the people around us. With the cultural and emotional meaning that drinking carries, letting go of alcohol can feel like a loaded decision that carries both emotional and social implications. This often creates what I call the social drinking loop.

The Invisible Social Drinking Loop

A social drinking loop is an unwanted or unhealthy drinking pattern that is driven by our innate human needs for connection and belonging and fueled by the belief that alcohol can help us connect or fit in. Through repetition, drinking becomes one of our default ways to fit in, to be part of the crowd, or to bring out the version of ourselves that we believe we need to be to be accepted and loved.

The Social Drinking Loop
Source: Jeanette Hu | Sober Curiosity

For most people who have come to question their drinking patterns, alcohol is only what's on the surface. Beneath, there are often many invisible loops that keep their current drinking patterns alive. A social drinking loop is one of the 10 most common drinking loops that can keep pulling a person back to their old drinking pattern even when they want to cut down or stop.

Like most invisible drinking loops, a social drinking loop starts as an attempt to meet a deep-seated need. However, over time, as the drinking loop deepens, it can gradually move us further away, instead of closer to the things that we need and deeply desire; in this case, real connection and true belonging.

The Difference Between Fitting In and Belonging

In the short run, fitting in can almost feel like belonging. When we fit in, we feel like we are a part of the group. We may feel accepted, welcomed, even liked. However, fitting in is different from belonging.

If belonging is being unconditionally accepted for who we are, then fitting in is being accepted on the condition that we act like everyone else.

Most of us can tell the difference instinctively. For me, it’s the difference between feeling at ease even when I’m quiet and having to put on my bubbly social mask; feeling comfortable ordering a hot tea instead of joining others with a cold beer; or talking about my nerdy science-fiction interests instead of pretending to be interested in fantasy football.

When we belong, we feel that we are welcomed for just being ourselves, and when we fit in, we feel like we have to perform to be accepted. I spent years confusing the two, believing that being liked meant I belonged.

The Near-Enemy Trap

Fitting in is what I call a near enemy of belonging—something that looks and feels like what we deeply desire, but can actually keep us from obtaining the real thing.

The paradox here is that we can’t fit in and belong at the same time, because we can’t try to act like someone else and be our true selves at the same time. When we drink to fit in, whether it's to drink what others drink, act the way others expect us to, or pretend to enjoy what others enjoy, we cover up our most authentic selves. We might fit in, but we feel like nobody knows the real us.

Authenticity as a Practice

As with most other drinking loops, simply removing alcohol is rarely the answer. To break the social drinking loop, we need to learn how to let go of the illusion of safety that fitting in provides in exchange for the courage to show up as our truer selves.

The 4-Pillar Sobriety System
Source: Jeanette Hu | Sober Curiosity

Of course, that's easier said than done. When we've spent years learning to fit in, showing up as our true selves can often feel like a skill we have not yet learned. That’s why, in my 4-Pillar system, skill expansion is one of the core pillars to build a joyful, fulfilling life beyond alcohol.

Fortunately, like most skills, showing up with more authenticity is something we can learn through practice. And sometimes, that practice can be as simple as learning to say “no” when we mean “no,” instead of automatically saying “yes” to fit in. If you'd like to give it a try, you can start with my 7 personal favorite, ready-to-use scripts for saying no with grace. It works not just for turning down a drink, but for saying no to other things in life, too.
